body:
Community and regional background

Padhar dance is a traditional folk dance of the Padhar community, a Scheduled Tribe of Gujarat. The community is particularly associated with villages surrounding Nal Sarovar in the Bhal region of Gujarat, extending across Ahmedabad and Surendranagar districts.

The traditional occupations of the Padhars include fishing and boating. Their relationship with water has influenced the imagery, themes and movements of their folk dances.

Distinctive characteristics

Padhar dance is recognised for movements that represent the rising and falling of waves and the rocking motion of boats. Such movements express the community's traditional livelihood and familiarity with aquatic environments.

Participants may perform close to the ground, adopting seated and low positions that evoke the movement of boats on water.

Musical instruments

The manjira, a pair of small metallic cymbals, is particularly characteristic of the Padhar dance tradition. The associated Manjira Nritya is well known in the Bhalnalkantha region.

Traditional Padhar Raas performed by male groups commonly uses manjira to maintain rhythm, with instruments such as tabla and zanz, or larger cymbals, providing accompaniment.

Some descriptions of Padhar Nritya also identify small sticks or dandiya. These descriptions reflect variation within Padhar dance traditions. Manjira remains the stronger identifying association for traditional Padhar Raas and Manjira Nritya.

Occasions and cultural expression

Padhar dances are performed at community gatherings, devotional occasions and cultural festivals. Traditional Padhar Raas includes devotional singing, including songs associated with Krishna.

The dance illustrates how a folk tradition can express occupational experiences and religious devotion at the same time.

Key geographical association

Padhar dance is associated with Nal Sarovar and the Bhal region, particularly Ahmedabad and Surendranagar districts. Its wave-like movements do not imply that the community is restricted to Gujarat's present-day seacoast.

Prelims focus

  • Padhar dance belongs to the Padhar community.
  • Nal Sarovar is its important geographical association.
  • Ahmedabad and Surendranagar are the associated districts.
  • Fishing and boating influence the dance's traditional imagery.
  • Manjira is its particularly characteristic instrument.
  • Trap: Padhar dance represents waves and boats, whereas Hudo reflects pastoral life.

[References: GCERT, Social Science, Standard 10, Chapter 2, p. 16; NCERT, India: Unity in Cultural Diversity, first edition, 2018, Gujarat, Table 1, p. 38; Government of Gujarat, Tribal Development Department, publication on tribal communities, section 7.6, Padhar, p. 127; Utpala Desai, Raas Traditions of Gujarat, Sahapedia, Padhar Raas; Jignisha Vaidya, The Unpopular Folk Dances of Gujarat State, in Bharatiya Lok Sanskriti Evam Lalit Kalaen, The Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda, pp. 169–171. Online sources consulted on 25 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: The Padhar community’s Nal Sarovar and Bhal setting connects fishing and boating to wave and boat movements in dance, with manjira rhythm.
pictures.caption: Padhar dance reflects the community's relationship with water.

title: Padhar Dance: Fishing Communities and the Nal Sarovar Region

body:
The Siddi community

Siddi Dhamal, also written as Siddi Dhamaal, is a distinctive folk dance of the Siddi community of Gujarat. The Siddis are an Indian community of African ancestry with a long history of settlement in Gujarat.

The dance preserves important elements of African-origin music and collective performance within the religious and social environment of Gujarat.

Geographical association

An important centre of Siddi Dhamal is Jambur village in the Gir region. Jambur is situated in Talala taluka of present-day Gir Somnath district.

Older descriptions may associate Talala and Jambur with the former undivided Junagadh district. For present-day district-based identification, Gir Somnath is the relevant district.

Siddi communities also live in other parts of Gujarat, and Dhamal is not restricted exclusively to Jambur.

Religious and social occasions

Dhamal has an important association with the Siddi community's Sufi religious traditions. It is performed during celebrations connected with revered saints and their shrines.

One important occasion is an Urs, the annual commemoration of a Sufi saint's death. Dhamal is also presented at community celebrations, tribal cultural festivals and public cultural programmes.

Instruments and identifying features

Powerful percussion, rhythmic group singing and energetic movements are distinctive features of Siddi Dhamal. Performers may imitate the calls and movements of animals and birds, and peacock feathers are also associated with the tradition.

Mashira

The Mashira, also spelt Mashiro or Mashira, is a characteristic rhythmic instrument or prop associated with Siddi Dhamal. It consists of a coconut shell containing cowrie shells or similar rattling material, enclosed in cloth.

When shaken, the shells produce a rhythmic sound that accompanies the dance.

Drums

Dhol and smaller drums provide the main percussion accompaniment. A small drum associated with the performance is also referred to as Dhamal. Local names and the selection of accompanying instruments can vary.

Distinctive community association

Siddi Dhamal is a folk tradition of Gujarat's African-origin Siddi community. Jambur and the Mashira are particularly useful identifiers.

Prelims focus

  • Dhamal is associated with the Siddi community.
  • The Siddis have African ancestry.
  • Jambur is in Talala taluka of Gir Somnath district.
  • Urs and Sufi shrine celebrations are important religious occasions.
  • Mashira is a coconut-shell rattle.
  • Trap: Mashira is associated with Siddi Dhamal, not Padhar dance.

[References: GCERT, Social Science, Standard 10, Chapter 2, Gujarati edition, Siddi Dhamal section, p. 16; NCERT, India: Unity in Cultural Diversity, first edition, 2018, Gujarat, Table 1, p. 38; Jignisha Vaidya, The Unpopular Folk Dances of Gujarat State, The Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda, p. 170; Census of India, District Census Handbook, Junagadh, 1981, Talala, Madhupur Jambur entry; Ministry of Panchayati Raj, SVAMITVA village records, Gir Somnath district, Talala, Madhupur Jambur; Ministry of Tribal Affairs, Press Information Bureau, promotion of Siddi Dance. Online sources consulted on 25 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Mashira is a cloth-enclosed coconut-shell rattle containing cowrie shells; dhol and smaller drums accompany Gujarat’s Siddi Dhamal.
pictures.caption: Mashira and drums are characteristic of Siddi Dhamal.

title: Siddi Dhamal: African-Origin Cultural Heritage in Gujarat

body:
Regional and community association

Dangi Nritya refers to the distinctive tribal dance traditions associated with Dang district in the forested and hilly region of southern Gujarat.

Dang has several tribal communities, including the Bhil, Kokna, Kunbi and Warli communities. These communities maintain diverse traditions of collective dance, music and ritual celebrations.

Dangi dance should therefore be understood as a regional tribal tradition rather than a dance belonging exclusively to one caste or tribe.

Distinctive features

A characteristic feature of Dangi Nritya is the formation of a connected group or chain. Men and women hold hands or link themselves together while performing coordinated rhythmic movements.

These formations distinguish Dangi dance from dances that depend principally on individual props, such as the Tippani implement or dandiya sticks.

Some Dangi traditions are known for their vigorous movement and collective formations. Particular regional dance patterns are also known as Chala.

Occasions

Dangi dances are traditionally performed during Holi, Diwali, weddings, religious ceremonies and community celebrations.

Dang Darbar

The Dang Darbar is an important annual cultural gathering held at Ahwa, the headquarters of Dang district, around the time of Holi.

Traditional tribal music, dance and community participation are prominent features of the gathering. It provides an important occasion for observing the diversity of the Dangi performing arts.

Musical instruments

Dangi dance traditions are accompanied by percussion and wind instruments. Drums maintain the collective rhythm, while local wind instruments provide melodic accompaniment.

  • Dhol: A percussion drum used in tribal celebrations.
  • Kahadya: A local shehnai-type wind instrument associated with a distinctive Dangi dance tradition.
  • Pavri: A traditional wind instrument associated particularly with the Pawari dance of Dang.

Pawari as a related Dangi tradition

Pawari dance, also called Pavri Nritya, takes its name from the wind instrument used in its performance. The instrument is traditionally made using materials such as cattle horn, wood and dried gourd.

It is associated with Dangi tribal communities, particularly the Kokna or Konkani, Kunbi and Warli communities. The dance has an important religious association with the worship of Dungardev, a sacred mountain deity, and is also performed at Dang Darbar and other celebrations.

Pawari is one specific tradition within the broader tribal performing arts of Dang. Not every Dangi dance is necessarily a Pawari dance.

Prelims focus

  • Dangi Nritya belongs to the tribal traditions of Dang district.
  • Bhil, Kokna, Kunbi and Warli are important associated communities.
  • Connected chains and coordinated group movements are distinctive features.
  • Dang Darbar is held at Ahwa around Holi.
  • Pavri is a traditional wind instrument associated with Pawari dance.
  • Trap: Dangi Nritya is broader than the particular Pawari dance tradition.

[References: GCERT, Social Science, Standard 10, Chapter 2, p. 15; NCERT, India: Unity in Cultural Diversity, first edition, 2018, Gujarat, Table 1, pp. 38–39; Jignisha Vaidya, The Unpopular Folk Dances of Gujarat State, The Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda, p. 168; District Dang, Government of Gujarat, Culture and Heritage, Kahadya Dance and Dang Darbar; Gujarat Tourism, Dang Darbar; Ministry of Tribal Affairs, ADI KALAKAR Portal, Pawari Dance, 27 June 2022. Online sources consulted on 25 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Dangi men and women dance in a connected chain with drum and wind musicians at Dang Darbar in Ahwa, backed by forested hills.
pictures.caption: Collective Dangi dance at Dang Darbar.

pictures.alt: Pawari sits within wider Dangi performing traditions and uses Pavri, while dhol and Kahadya feature across the wider traditions.
pictures.caption: Pawari is a specific dance tradition within Dang's wider performing arts.

title: Dangi Dance: Tribal Traditions of Southern Gujarat

body:
Dance, community and geographical association

Gujarat's folk dances can be distinguished through their principal community associations and geographical centres. Garba and Raas have become widespread across the state, while Tippani, Hudo, Padhar, Siddi Dhamal and Dangi retain particularly distinctive regional and community identities.

DancePrincipal communityRegion or district
GarbaBroad participation across Gujarati communitiesThroughout Gujarat
RaasVarious Gujarati communitiesSaurashtra, Kachchh and other parts of Gujarat
TippaniTraditionally women of Koli, Kharva, Bhil and other working communitiesChorwad–Veraval coastal belt; Junagadh and Gir Somnath
HudoParticularly BharwadTarnetar and Panchal region; Surendranagar
PadharPadhar tribal communityNal Sarovar and Bhal; Ahmedabad and Surendranagar
Siddi DhamalAfrican-origin Siddi communityJambur, Talala; Gir Somnath
DangiBhil, Kokna, Kunbi, Warli and other Dangi tribal communitiesDang district, southern Gujarat

The places in this table indicate important traditional centres rather than exclusive geographical limits.

Occasions and characteristic features

DanceImportant occasionsInstrument or propIdentifying feature
GarbaNavratriEarthen lamp pot, dholShakti worship
RaasNavratri, Janmashtami, weddingsDandiya sticks in Dandiya RaasKrishna and Raas Leela
TippaniWeddings, festivalsTippani implementRhythmic striking of the ground
HudoTarnetar Fair, weddingsDholak, manjira, handclappingMovements inspired by sheep fights
PadharCommunity and devotional gatheringsManjiraWave-like and boat-like movements
Siddi DhamalUrs, shrine and cultural celebrationsMashira, drumsAfrican-origin community tradition
DangiHoli, weddings, Dang DarbarDhol and local wind instrumentsConnected group formations

Important distinctions for statement-based questions

Religious associations

Garba is principally associated with Shakti worship, whereas Raas has a particularly strong association with Krishna devotion. Both are performed during Navratri. Therefore, Navratri alone does not distinguish them.

Occupational associations

  • Tippani represents construction and floor-compacting labour.
  • Hudo represents the pastoral life of shepherds.
  • Padhar reflects fishing, boating and the aquatic environment.

Traditional participation

Tippani is traditionally female-dominated. Hudo traditionally involves both men and women. Traditional Padhar Raas groups are commonly male, whereas contemporary Garba and Dandiya Raas involve broad participation by both men and women.

Geographical distinctions

Surendranagar district is associated with both Hudo and Padhar traditions. Hudo is particularly linked with Tarnetar, while Padhar dance is linked with the Nal Sarovar region.

Gir Somnath district is associated with both the coastal Tippani tradition around Veraval and the Siddi Dhamal tradition at Jambur. Their communities and origins are entirely different.

Instrument and prop distinctions

Dhol and manjira are used in several Gujarati folk dances. More distinctive associations include the Tippani implement with Tippani, the Mashira with Siddi Dhamal, manjira with traditional Padhar Raas, and Pavri with the Pawari tradition of Dang.

International recognition

Among the 7 dance forms considered here, the UNESCO inscription is specifically named Garba of Gujarat. It was added to the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity on 6 December 2023, as India's 15th inscription at that time.

Prelims focus

  • Garba: Shakti, Navratri and UNESCO inscription in 2023.
  • Raas: Krishna devotion and Dandiya Raas.
  • Tippani: women, construction labour and the Chorwad–Veraval belt.
  • Hudo: Bharwad, Tarnetar and pastoral life.
  • Padhar: Nal Sarovar, fishing and manjira.
  • Siddi Dhamal: Jambur and Mashira; Dangi: Dang, Holi and connected tribal group formations.

One-glance revision

[References: GCERT, Social Science, Standard 10, Chapter 2, pp. 15–16; NCERT, India: Unity in Cultural Diversity, first edition, 2018, Gujarat, Table 1, pp. 38–39; UNESCO, Garba of Gujarat, Decision 18.COM 8.b.32; Utpala Desai, Raas Traditions of Gujarat, Sahapedia; The Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda, Bharatiya Lok Kalakar, pp. 215–216; The Unpopular Folk Dances of Gujarat State, in Bharatiya Lok Sanskriti Evam Lalit Kalaen, pp. 168–171; Gujarat Tourism, Dang Darbar and Tarnetar Fair; Ministry of Tribal Affairs, ADI KALAKAR Portal, Pawari Dance.
